content: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a clinical syndrome caused by an imbalance in the vaginal microbiota, commonly referred to as the vaginal flora. The vaginal flora is predominantly composed of Lactobacilli, which are essential for maintaining the health of the female genital tract by regulating the vaginal pH. A normal vaginal pH is typically less than 4.5, and this acidic environment inhibits the overgrowth of pathogenic microorganisms. When the vaginal pH becomes elevated, it creates an environment conducive to the proliferation of certain bacteria, leading to a low-grade infection characterized by abnormal vaginal discharge. BV must be distinguished from other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as purulent, malodorous, and thin vaginal discharge with an elevated vaginal pH. These conditions include trichomoniasis, atrophic vaginitis, and desquamative inflammatory vaginitis. Additionally, BV should be differentiated from vaginal candidiasis, vaginitis, and cervicitis. BV is the most common cause of vaginal symptoms in women, although the role of sexual activity in its development remains unclear. In the United States, the prevalence of BV is estimated to be 29.2% among women aged 14–49 years, affecting approximately 21.2 million individuals. If left untreated, BV can lead to significant complications, including premature delivery, postpartum infections, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), post-surgical complications (e.g., after abortion, hysterectomy, or cesarean section), increased susceptibility to HIV infection, and, in some cases, infertility. Antimicrobial therapy is recommended for all symptomatic women and for asymptomatic pregnant women at high risk of complications. Metronidazole is the preferred treatment for pregnant patients. Historically, the role of bacterial flora in vaginal infections was first hypothesized by Albert Döderlein in 1892. In 1955, Gardner and Dukes identified Haemophilus vaginalis (now known as Gardnerella vaginalis) as a causative agent of foul-smelling, watery vaginal discharge. The pathophysiology of BV involves a disruption of the normal vaginal flora, which is predominantly composed of Gram-positive Lactobacilli. These bacteria maintain the vaginal pH at acidic levels, preventing the overgrowth of pathogenic microorganisms. When the vaginal pH becomes elevated, opportunistic bacteria such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, Ureaplasma, and anaerobes can proliferate, leading to the characteristic symptoms of BV. The differential diagnosis of BV includes other conditions that cause similar symptoms, such as trichomoniasis, atrophic vaginitis, desquamative inflammatory vaginitis, vaginal candidiasis, vaginitis, and cervicitis. BV is the most common cause of vaginal symptoms in women, but the exact role of sexual activity in its pathogenesis remains uncertain. Risk factors for BV include sexual activity, having a new or multiple sexual partners, being a woman who has sex with women, the presence of other sexually transmitted infections, douching, and cigarette smoking. Routine screening for BV is not recommended for asymptomatic women, including pregnant women, as there is insufficient evidence to support its role in preventing preterm birth. However, symptomatic women and high-risk pregnant women should be evaluated and treated. The natural history of BV indicates that many women are asymptomatic. Symptomatic patients may report vaginal odor and thin, white or gray vaginal discharge. If untreated, BV can progress to more severe conditions, including salpingitis, endometritis, bacteremia, and PID. In pregnant women, untreated BV can lead to complications such as premature rupture of membranes, preterm labor, chorioamnionitis, postpartum endometritis, and septic abortion. The diagnosis of BV is based on clinical criteria, specifically the Amsel criteria, which require the presence of at least three of the following four findings: thin, gray or white vaginal discharge; a malodorous, fishy odor upon the addition of 10% potassium hydroxide; a vaginal pH greater than 4.5; and the presence of clue cells on microscopic examination. A detailed sexual history is essential for diagnosis, focusing on the number and type of sexual partners and any history of sexually transmitted infections. Approximately 50–75% of women with BV are asymptomatic, but common symptoms include thin, white or gray vaginal discharge and an unpleasant vaginal odor, particularly after sexual intercourse. Physical examination findings in BV typically include a fishy vaginal odor, thin white or gray discharge, and an absence of significant vulvovaginal inflammation. Laboratory diagnosis can be made using Amsel’s criteria or Gram stain, the latter being the gold standard. Other diagnostic tests include the Affirm VP III test, the OSOM BVBlue system, and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Imaging studies are not relevant for the diagnosis of BV. Treatment of BV involves antimicrobial therapy, with metronidazole being the drug of choice, particularly for pregnant patients. Primary prevention strategies include limiting the number of sexual partners, avoiding douching, and using condoms or estrogen-containing contraceptives.5, bacteriotherapy, avoiding douching, and modifying contraceptive methods.
